extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientometricians, and funding-agency staff interested in grant peer review quality and psychometrics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the quality of grant peer review using classical psychometric criteria (reliability, fairness, validity) and the SNSF review dimensions for biology and medicine applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement between reviewers on the same application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured using intraclass correlation (ICC). Reinhart reports ICC ≈ 0.41 overall (interpreted as fair but low), ICC ≈ 0.45 for biology, and ICC ≈ 0.20 for medicine (strikingly poorer agreement). Implication: assess inter-rater agreement quantitatively and account for field-specific differences; consider calibration or reviewer training where agreement is low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of bias of funding decisions with respect to applicant characteristics irrelevant to scientific merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tested via multiple logistic regression on funding decisions using predictors: applicant gender, age, nationality, academic status/rank, requested funding amount, and institutional affiliation. Reinhart found none of these were significant predictors — funding aligned with scientific performance indicators. Guidance: include demographic and institutional variables in bias tests; interpret null findings in context and consider study power and sample/field limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictive accuracy of peer review/funding decisions for future research outcomes (e.g., bibliometric performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize validity by comparing funding outcomes to subsequent bibliometric measures of applicant performance. Reinhart finds only weak prediction at the individual-proposal level (though aggregate funding aligns with publication success). Guidance: recognize that predictive signal exists but is noisy; avoid overclaiming precision of selection decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality / originality of the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the proposal's scientific quality and originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as an explicit SNSF evaluation criterion during the study period. Reviewers should assess novelty, conceptual contribution, and advancement of knowledge. This criterion is a primary driver of decisions alongside methodology and applicant performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the proposed research methods and their appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the SNSF rubric: reviewers evaluate whether the methodology is rigorous, suitable to the research question, and likely to produce valid results. Poor or unclear methods reduce scores regardless of applicant reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility / work plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical feasibility of the project and quality of the work plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in the SNSF rubric: reviewers judge timeline, resource allocation, and whether the proposed work is realistic given the requested funding and team. Feasibility concerns can weigh heavily in funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant track record
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the applicant's prior scientific performance and CV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SNSF reviewers consider publication record and other performance indicators. Reinhart's analysis found scientific performance indicators drive funding decisions; incorporate objective measures (publications, citations, prior grants) while being mindful of field differences and career stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of expected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance and expected impact of the proposed research outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of SNSF rubric: consider potential contribution to the field, translational or societal impact, and whether expected results justify funding. High-impact expected results can offset moderate methodological weaknesses when plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scientific performance indicators / bibliometrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bibliometric or other performance indicators as predictors or correlates of funding decisions and future success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinhart shows that scientific performance indicators were the only significant predictors of funding decisions in the models tested. However, validity analyses indicate these indicators only weakly predict future bibliometric performance at the individual-proposal level. Guidance: use bibliometrics as one input but interpret cautiously and complement with qualitative assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-specific calibration of review rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust rubrics and reviewer processes to account for differences across research fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reliability differed markedly between biology and medicine (ICC 0.45 vs. 0.20), the study implies rubrics and reviewer training should be calibrated by field/subdiscipline. Consider different evaluation weightings, reviewer selection, or additional corroborating evidence in low-agreement fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overclaiming precision of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Design rubrics and interpret review scores with acknowledgment of the limited signal-to-noise ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given modest validity (weak prediction of individual outcomes) and only fair reliability, funding agencies should not frame review outcomes as highly precise predictors of future success. Recommendations: communicate uncertainty, use multiple indicators, and avoid binary interpretations based solely on small score differences.
